Defining the True Cost of Clinical AI Beyond Vendor Bills

Clinical artificial intelligence is becoming increasingly embedded within electronic health record workflows, yet defining the true cost of these technologies remains difficult for health systems, according to an analysis by Vishva Natarajan, Caleb Stewart, Jennifer Hong, and Saeed Hassanpour published in PLOS Digital Health. Although healthcare organizations are rapidly adopting these automated tools, the researchers report that the direct bill presented by commercial vendors often fails to capture the full scope of financial resources necessary to deploy, maintain, and support them.

Healthcare institutions currently finance clinical AI through several distinct payment models, including usage-based services, subscription contracts, enterprise licenses, local hosting arrangements, or hybrid combinations of these methods. Usage-based pricing creates unique operational challenges because the billing units—such as individual tokens or billable user sessions—are determined by vendors rather than standard metrics. Furthermore, these vendor-defined metrics can vary across different data modalities, languages, and timeframes, complicating budget predictability.

Alternative contracting mechanisms shift the nature of these expenditures rather than eliminating financial ambiguity. Fixed licensing agreements and enterprise subscriptions can make recurring vendor charges more predictable, while locally hosted artificial intelligence models redistribute organizational spending directly toward internal technical infrastructure and personnel.

Regardless of the overarching payment structure selected, the comprehensive resources required to operate and maintain clinical artificial intelligence remain difficult to capture. Substantial resources must support engineering, continuous validation, governance oversight, and securing rights to clinical data. Looking ahead, the researchers note that as the complexity of multimodal and agentic systems increases, the associated payment structures will become equally complex.

To ensure that artificial intelligence does not become another driver of healthcare spending detached from delivered value, health systems must take proactive measures. The authors conclude that organizations will need to establish methods to measure AI costs accurately, evaluate its clinical value, and negotiate vendor agreements that allow for regular reassessment of prices and contract terms.

Subject of Research: Healthcare economics and pricing structures of clinical artificial intelligence

Article Title: Paying for clinical AI: The bill is not the cost

Article References: Natarajan, V., Stewart, C., Hong, J., & Hassanpour, S. (2026). Paying for clinical AI: The bill is not the cost. PLOS Digital Health, 5(11), e0001814. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pdig.0001814
